guide.title: Atlanta Weekends from Dahlonega to Savannah
guide.author: friends of Placemoir
guide.summary: Six weekend trips from Atlanta, from the North Georgia mountains and Athens to Chattanooga, Highlands and Savannah, each with a place to stay, two places to eat and a few things to do.

places.name: Hall House Hotel
places.notes: A small hotel in an 1880s building right on the town square, so everything in Dahlonega is a short walk. Rooms are upstairs over the shops and restaurants.

places.name: Amicalola Falls Lodge
places.address: 418 Amicalola Falls Lodge Road, Dawsonville, GA 30534
places.notes: The state park lodge sits on the mountain above the falls, about half an hour west of Dahlonega. Walk out the door to the trails and the long view toward Atlanta.

places.name: Back Porch Oyster Bar
places.notes: Oysters, shrimp and seafood pastas a few steps off the square. Ask for the porch when the weather is good.

places.name: Montaluce Winery & Restaurant
places.notes: A Tuscan-style winery a few miles outside town with a tasting room and a restaurant overlooking the vines. Book ahead for weekend brunch or dinner.

places.name: Dahlonega Gold Museum State Historic Site
places.notes: The 1836 courthouse in the middle of the square tells the story of the 1829 gold rush and the branch mint that once struck coins in town.

places.name: Amicalola Falls State Park
places.address: 166 Amicalola Falls State Park Rd, Dawsonville, GA 30534
places.notes: One of the tallest waterfalls in the Southeast, with a staircase climb beside it and an approach trail to the start of the Appalachian Trail. Parking fees apply; check the official site.

places.name: Rivet House
places.notes: A boutique hotel in a converted factory building at the old Southern Mill complex, northwest of downtown, with an Italian restaurant and a small spa on site. Downtown is a short drive or ride-share away.

places.name: Five & Ten
places.notes: A long-running Athens dinner spot in a house on Milledge Avenue, cooking Southern food with local farm produce. Save it for a Saturday night and reserve ahead.

places.name: The National
places.notes: A downtown neighborhood restaurant with Mediterranean-leaning plates, a good bar and a patio. Easy for lunch between walks around campus.

places.name: State Botanical Garden of Georgia
places.notes: The university's garden south of town, with a glass conservatory, themed gardens and miles of wooded trails along the Middle Oconee River.

places.name: Georgia Museum of Art
places.notes: The official state art museum, on the university's east campus, with a strong collection of American paintings and decorative arts from the South.

places.name: Blue Ridge Inn Bed & Breakfast
places.address: 477 W First St, Blue Ridge, GA 30513
places.notes: An 1890 Victorian house a block from downtown, with a wraparound porch and a cooked breakfast. A good alternative to renting a cabin up a mountain road.

places.name: Harvest on Main
places.address: 576 E Main St, Blue Ridge, GA 30513
places.notes: A Main Street dinner and lunch spot built around local sourcing: grass-fed beef from nearby farms, seasonal vegetables and North Georgia trout, with a long wine list.

places.name: Black Sheep Restaurant
places.address: 480 W Main St, Blue Ridge, GA 30513
places.notes: Dinner and weekend brunch in an old house with a big covered patio and outdoor bar under the oaks.

places.name: Blue Ridge Scenic Railway
places.notes: A train from the downtown depot along the Toccoa River to McCaysville, where you can step across the Tennessee line before riding back. Book ahead for fall color weekends.

places.name: Mercier Orchards
places.address: 8660 Blue Ridge Dr, Blue Ridge, GA 30513
places.notes: A family orchard north of town with a big market, a bakery known for fried pies, hard cider and pick-your-own seasons for berries and apples.

places.name: Toccoa River Swinging Bridge
places.address: Forest Service Road 816, off Aska Road, Blue Ridge, GA 30513
places.notes: A long suspension footbridge over the Toccoa on the Benton MacKaye Trail, a short walk from a gravel forest road lot. The road is rough, so higher clearance helps.

places.name: The Read House
places.notes: Chattanooga's grand 1920s hotel downtown, restored with a dark-wood lobby bar and a steakhouse. Walkable to the Southside and a short ride to the river.

places.name: The Dwell Hotel
places.notes: A small hotel in an early 1900s building downtown, with each room decorated differently and a bright solarium cafe downstairs.

places.name: Main Street Meats
places.notes: A Southside butcher shop with a restaurant attached, known for its burger, house charcuterie and steaks cut in-house.

places.name: St. John's Restaurant
places.notes: Chattanooga's longtime special-occasion dinner, cooking regional American food with local ingredients. It has moved downtown to Chestnut Street, so ignore older listings on Market Street.

places.name: Tennessee Aquarium
places.notes: Two buildings on the riverfront: one follows a raindrop from the Appalachian headwaters down the Tennessee River, the other covers the oceans. Give it half a day.

places.name: Walnut Street Bridge
places.notes: An 1890s truss bridge now open only to people on foot and bikes, linking downtown with the North Shore's shops and Coolidge Park. Best at sunset.

places.name: Rock City Gardens
places.notes: The old roadside attraction on top of Lookout Mountain, just over the Georgia line: a path through sandstone formations, a swinging bridge and Lover's Leap with its view across several states.

places.name: Old Edwards Inn and Spa
places.notes: The splurge stay in Highlands, a restored 1870s inn on Main Street with a full spa and rooms spread across several buildings in town.

places.name: Highlander Mountain House
places.notes: A relaxed, more affordable stay on Main Street styled like an English country house, with fires in the common rooms, a pet-friendly bunkhouse out back and a tavern for dinner.

places.name: Madison's Restaurant
places.notes: The dining room off the Old Edwards lobby, cooking with produce from the inn's own farm. Worth a dinner even if you stay elsewhere; reserve ahead.

places.name: Mountain Fresh Grocery
places.notes: A grocery, deli, bakery and coffee bar where you can grab breakfast or build a trail lunch before heading out to the overlooks.

places.name: Whiteside Mountain Trail
places.notes: A two-mile loop to the top of sheer granite cliffs, with long views over the Chattooga valley. There is a small parking fee at the trailhead.

places.name: Dry Falls
places.notes: A short paved path and stairs lead behind a waterfall in the Cullasaja Gorge, so you can stand under the overhang and stay mostly dry. Check the Forest Service site for closures.

places.name: The Marshall House
places.notes: An 1850s hotel on Broughton Street with iron balconies, a central location between the river and the squares, and plenty of ghost stories.

places.name: The Thunderbird Inn
places.notes: A 1960s motor inn redone in retro colors at the west edge of the historic district. The budget pick, with parking and an easy walk to City Market.

places.name: Mrs. Wilkes' Dining Room
places.notes: Weekday lunch served family-style at shared tables, bowls of fried chicken and Southern sides passed around with strangers. Expect a line, bring cash, and note the winter break.

places.name: The Grey
places.address: 109 Martin Luther King Jr Blvd, Savannah, GA 31401
places.notes: A restored 1938 Greyhound bus station where the kitchen cooks Southern food through a Savannah port-city lens. Reserve well ahead for dinner.

places.name: Forsyth Park
places.address: Gaston St & Whitaker St, Savannah, GA 31401
places.notes: The big green at the south end of the historic district, with its fountain, live oaks and a Saturday farmers market. Walk up through the squares to get there.

places.name: Bonaventure Cemetery
places.notes: A Victorian cemetery on a bluff over the Wilmington River, with moss-draped oaks and carved monuments. Pick up a map at the gate and go early in the day.

places.name: Wormsloe State Historic Site
places.notes: A long avenue of live oaks leads to the tabby ruins of an 18th-century colonial estate, with marsh trails and a small museum.
